title: Calculate the total cost of several items (to $100)

lesson.title: Adding Up What You Buy

steps.say: You already know how to add decimals by lining up the decimal point. Today we use that same trick for something real: figuring out the total cost when you buy a few things at the store.

Here is the idea. Every price is its own little bar, and the total is all the bars pushed together into one long bar. So to find a total cost, you just add the prices, one at a time. Let us shop for school supplies in Kelowna: a notebook for four dollars and twenty-five cents, a water bottle for twelve dollars and fifty cents, and a backpack for twenty-eight dollars and seventy-five cents.

visual.caption: Three prices — push them together to get the total

steps.say: Step one: add the first two prices. Write them one above the other with the decimal points lined up in a straight column, then add. Twenty-five cents plus fifty cents is seventy-five cents, and four dollars plus twelve dollars is sixteen dollars. So the notebook and the bottle together cost sixteen dollars and seventy-five cents.

Step two: take that running total and add the next price. Sixteen dollars and seventy-five cents plus twenty-eight dollars and seventy-five cents. Seventy-five cents plus seventy-five cents is one dollar and fifty cents, so we carry that one dollar over. Sixteen plus twenty-eight is forty-four, plus the carried dollar makes forty-five. The total is forty-five dollars and fifty cents.

visual.caption: Jump from 16.75 up by 28.75 to land on 45.50

steps.say: Here is a mistake lots of kids make. They add all the dollars to get forty-four, then add all the cents, twenty-five plus fifty plus seventy-five, and get one hundred fifty cents, and write forty-four dollars and one hundred fifty cents. But you can never have one hundred fifty cents sitting in the cents spot! One hundred cents is a whole dollar, so trade it: forty-four dollars plus one more dollar is forty-five, and fifty cents is left over. Forty-five dollars and fifty cents — the same answer as before.
So remember: stack the prices with the decimal points lined up, add them one at a time, and trade every hundred cents for one dollar.

lesson.answer: To find a total cost, line up the decimal points and add the prices one at a time — and trade every 100 cents for 1 dollar.

practice.question: You are picking up groceries in Victoria. A bag of apples costs five dollars and forty cents, a block of cheese costs nine dollars and seventy-five cents, and a loaf of bread costs three dollars and eighty-five cents. Write the three prices in a stack with the decimal points lined up and add them. What is the total cost?
practice.answer: Nineteen dollars, written as 19.00 — because 5.40 plus 9.75 is 15.15, and 15.15 plus 3.85 is 19.00.
